title: +62% Since May 2025: Record Sales, Still A BUY
description: $67 target unchanged. AI wins strengthen the thesis, but margins need to recover.
body_html:
The position is up +62% since I picked it in May 2025. My position has not changed, and neither has my $67 target.

If you missed the beginning, here is the original May 2025 pick.

The idea was straightforward: a customer service outsourcer was winning business, improving its delivery model, and using AI to make its offering more useful.

The latest earnings give that thesis more substance. Revenue hit another record, new client wins accelerated, and management expects another year of growth. But Q4 also exposed that more revenue did not translate into more operating profit.

Behind the paywall, I revisit the original thesis, walk through the presentation’s AI case studies, and explain why I still rate the shares BUY. I also separate the promising industry trends from the ways automation could hurt the economics.

In this update

  • How the company ranks

  • What Q4 changed

  • Pillar #1. Client wins and healthier revenue mix: Confirmed

  • Pillar #2. Offshore delivery and margin expansion: Challenged

  • Pillar #3. AI as a source of business: Evolving

  • The industry outlook: implementation work grows, routine work shrinks

  • Pillar #4. Cash generation and capital allocation: Evolving

  • Pillar #5. Valuation leaves room for growth: Confirmed, with less cushion

  • The Monte Carlo: 10,000 illustrative runs

  • What could change my mind

  • Still a BUY

TLDR

  • IBEX Limited [] remains a BUY, with an unchanged $67 target and no change to my position.

  • FY2026 revenue grew 15.4% y/y; FY2027 guidance implies roughly 10% growth at the midpoint.

  • Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin fell to 12.3% from 13.9%. Client ramps must start converting into better profitability.

  • AI is producing client wins and measurable operating results, but it can also reduce the human work IBEX bills for.

  • Cash generation and capital returns support the thesis. Dilution, tax normalization, and customer concentration still matter.

How the company ranks

IBEX scores 74 on RankedStocks.com, with profitability its strongest factor and outlook its weakest.

That is a fair starting point for this update. The company has demonstrated good returns on capital and improving sales. The market’s expectations still deserve scrutiny.

The profitability detail is particularly useful. Returns on equity, assets, and invested capital score much better than the operating margins themselves. IBEX’s appeal comes partly from how efficiently it uses its asset base. It does not need software margins to create value.

The growth score reflects strong recent operating progress. I put more weight on reported revenue and cash flow than on the provider’s forward EPS estimates, which depend on the estimate set and timing. My FY2027 forecast follows management’s guidance.

You can run the same screens on RankedStocks.com for free. I have also added a new ROIC vs. WACC graph, which I will use below to examine whether growth is creating value.

What Q4 changed

FY2026 was a good year. Revenue reached $644.1M, and adjusted EPS grew 28%. Q4 was IBEX’s sixth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth.

The annual numbers confirm that the sales recovery in the original article continued. They also show why I want to separate business progress from the EPS headline. Lower taxes and a lower weighted-average diluted share count helped earnings per share.

Q4 was more mixed. Revenue rose 11.6% y/y, while GAAP EPS fell to $0.59 from $0.66. Adjusted EPS also slipped, to $0.85 from $0.87.

The earnings release points to training expenses, work moving between delivery locations, and higher fuel costs. Some of that spending supports future revenue. But the costs are real today, and a larger sales base should eventually produce more profit.

That is the central question for FY2027.

Pillar #1. Client wins and healthier revenue mix: Confirmed

Original thesis: Growth in better verticals and larger client relationships would offset the drag from legacy telecom work.

What changed: HealthTech has become a meaningful growth engine. Q4 revenue in that vertical grew 42%, reaching 17.9% of the quarter’s total. Technology and travel, transportation, and logistics also grew strongly.

HealthTech’s roughly 38% full-year growth does not mean it represents 38% of IBEX. It remains under one-fifth of sales, leaving room for the vertical to matter more if the client ramps continue.

IBEX also won 17 clients during FY2026, including nine in Q4. The company’s revenue retention measure remained above 99%. Together, those figures support growth through both existing relationships and new business.

My assessment: This pillar has held up well. I was right that the legacy telecom business would become less important to the overall growth rate. I am more interested now in whether the newer relationships can reach attractive margins.

Diversification has improved, although it is still a concentrated business. The largest client represented 9% of Q4 revenue, and the top five represented one-third.

Those are better proportions, but losing a large account would still hurt. Client wins reduce that dependence gradually. They do not make it disappear.

Pillar #2. Offshore delivery and margin expansion: Challenged

Original thesis: A more efficient delivery footprint, better utilization, and technology would expand margins as revenue grew.

What changed: Annual adjusted EBITDA rose, but its margin was slightly lower. Q4’s decline was more pronounced.

The quarterly picture makes the issue clearer. Adjusted EBITDA was slightly below the prior year despite double-digit revenue growth.

I was too optimistic about how smoothly growth would flow through to margins. Hiring and training people before a contract reaches full production can depress earnings. Moving work offshore can also temporarily duplicate costs. That explanation is plausible, but the following quarters must demonstrate the payoff.

The delivery story has also become more nuanced. Offshore operations remained important, while onshore revenue grew faster during FY2026, supported by HealthTech, AI offerings, and digital acquisition. Geography alone is becoming a less useful guide to the economics; the service mix matters too.

My assessment: I still expect modest improvement, but I have reduced the weight I put on automatic margin expansion. The current forecast assumes gradual gains from utilization and mix, with continued investment.

The quarter’s restructuring and impairment charges do not explain away the decline in adjusted EBITDA margin. Those adjustments are already excluded from that measure.

Pillar #3. AI as a source of business: Evolving

Original thesis: IBEX could use AI to improve service quality, retain clients, and win work.

What changed: There are now specific deployments to evaluate. The Sierra partnership combines a conversational AI platform with IBEX’s operating knowledge and integration work.

The partnership announcement helps explain the commercial proposition. A client needs more than a bot that can answer a question. It needs access to the right systems, clear escalation rules, and a process that works when the answer is complicated.

The case studies are the strongest new evidence in the deck.

Philippine Airlines’ initial resolution rate was 24%, with a customer satisfaction score of 4.71 out of five. BJ’s Wholesale Club was a new client won through the AI offering. Its initial resolution rate was higher, with a similarly strong satisfaction score.

The luxury activewear example is especially interesting. IBEX says it won the relationship through Sierra and is scaling human support alongside the AI solution. That is a practical example of automation helping IBEX enter an account.

The digital acquisition case also shows a revenue opportunity beyond reducing service costs. Management expects more than $3M of incremental FY2027 revenue from that deployment. I treat that as an expectation within the company’s outlook, rather than adding a separate AI bonus to my forecast.

My assessment: The AI case is stronger than it was in May 2025. It is still early to know how much profit IBEX will retain from these services or how durable that advantage will be.

A resolution rate measures tasks handled by AI. It does not translate directly into the same percentage of lost IBEX revenue. Pricing, implementation work, new client wins, and the remaining human workload all affect the result. Equally, higher automation does not automatically mean higher revenue.

The next useful disclosure would be the revenue and margin contribution from AI services, together with the effect on existing human work. The current presentation demonstrates adoption more clearly than it demonstrates the consolidated profit contribution.

The industry outlook: implementation work grows, routine work shrinks

IBEX’s results sit within a divided industry. TaskUs [] reported Q2 revenue growth of 5%, with AI Services growing 25.8% and digital customer experience growing 6.4%. Its adjusted EBITDA margin still declined. Growing AI demand and pressure on profitability can occur together.

Concentrix Corporation [] reported only 1.9% revenue growth in its quarter ended May. Its adjusted EBITDA margin also fell. These businesses have different client mixes and fiscal calendars, but IBEX’s faster growth stands out against those results.

My industry outlook has two parts. Demand for implementing and operating AI systems should grow as companies move beyond pilots. Routine customer contacts are also becoming easier to automate, putting pressure on contracts priced around people and time.

McKinsey’s customer care research helps explain the opportunity. The gap between leading and lagging organizations leaves room for providers that can turn AI pilots into dependable service operations.

The adoption gap gives IBEX a potential opening with clients that need help integrating AI into daily operations. I think its experience running customer service can matter here: clients need working escalation rules, quality controls, and access to their own systems. The Sierra partnership addresses that need, although the chart does not establish that IBEX has a lasting advantage over competing providers.

The efficiency gains also expose the risk to IBEX. Shorter handling times can reduce billable hours even when contact volumes keep growing. These bars mix expectations for the next 12-24 months with reported customer-experience changes over the past year; they are not a forecast of BPO revenue. For IBEX, the commercial test is whether implementation fees, ongoing AI services, and new accounts offset the human hours clients no longer need.

Comfort with autonomous service is another constraint on adoption. I expect providers to earn trust through reliable resolutions and clear accountability when something goes wrong. IBEX’s early client deployments are relevant evidence, but the survey measures executives’ confidence, so it cannot tell us how much revenue IBEX will capture.

Human support still has a role, particularly when customers want reassurance or their problem remains unresolved. The percentages here represent executives identifying barriers, not the share of consumers who reject AI. For IBEX, I see an opportunity to manage the handoff between automation and people. That could protect client relationships, although the remaining cases may be harder and more expensive to handle.

For IBEX, the opportunity is to earn more of a client’s total service budget even as each interaction requires less human effort. That requires effective delivery and contracts that reward the broader service. It is a more demanding business than simply adding seats.

The BPO comparison puts IBEX at the top of this group overall. Its profitability score is close to TASK’s, while its growth score trails ExlService Holdings []. But IBEX is not the cheapest name on the screen: TASK and CNXC score better on valuation. IBEX’s projected EBIT margin is also below the peers with estimates shown. I read that as a business with strong capital efficiency and improving demand, but room to improve operating margins. The BUY case depends on converting growth into cash and profit; a high overall score alone does not establish undervaluation.

Pillar #4. Cash generation and capital allocation: Evolving

Original thesis: Better operations and buybacks would increase value per share.

What changed: IBEX generated record FCF while spending more on capacity and technology. The presentation puts the reinvestment requirement beside the cash result.

Operating cash flow grew faster than FCF because capital spending increased. FCF of $31.2M was about 38% of adjusted EBITDA. That is useful cash generation, but it leaves a substantial gap between the profit measure used in guidance and cash available after investment.

Q4’s strong cash result also benefited from collections. I am using 73 receivable days in the forecast, consistent with management’s low-to-mid-70s outlook, rather than assuming the quarter-end 69 days becomes permanent. The tax forecast uses 21%, the midpoint of management’s normalized range. FY2026’s reported tax benefit should not be repeated automatically.

The balance sheet gives IBEX room to fund growth without relying on a large borrowing program.

My assessment: The cash position strengthens the thesis. I am less impressed by gross repurchases alone. IBEX spent $14.4M buying shares during the year, while stock compensation remained a meaningful cost.

The reconciliation makes that cost visible.

SBC increased to $7.7M. I retain a recurring stock compensation expense in the valuation. The FY2026 annual filing also shows that year-end shares outstanding fell only modestly despite the repurchases. The remaining buyback authorization is an option.

A new way to see the capital returns

I added a new ROIC vs. WACC graph to RankedStocks.com. It compares returns on invested capital with the estimated cost of that capital.

For IBEX, the sustained positive spread is more persuasive than one strong year’s EPS. It supports the idea that the business can reinvest productively.

The chart uses the platform’s historical estimates and definitions. Its WACC line is different from the 8.6% forward discount rate in my DCF, and its ROIC should not be read as identical to every return metric in the model. The useful observation is the persistence of returns above estimated capital costs.

That is evidence in favor of funding growth. Future projects still have to earn those returns.

Pillar #5. Valuation leaves room for growth: Confirmed, with less cushion

Original thesis: The business was worth more than the market price implied, even with restrained growth assumptions.

What changed: Sales have exceeded the modest growth path I originally discussed. The share price has also risen, reducing the gap to my unchanged target.

FY2027 guidance calls for revenue of $700M to $715M and adjusted EBITDA of $90M to $94M. At the midpoints, that implies about 10% revenue growth and a 13% adjusted EBITDA margin. It asks for modest profitability improvement, rather than a dramatic jump.

My $67 target remains unchanged. The revised DCF uses a 4.8% risk-free rate and a 4.23% equity market risk premium, producing an 8.6% WACC. That is above the 7.2% discount rate in the original article, while the forecast now starts from a substantially larger business.

My assessment: The valuation still supports BUY. Check my DCF here. The forecast follows the FY2027 guidance midpoints, then slows toward 2% long-term growth. It allows modest margin recovery and ongoing capital spending.

At the model’s $39.44 quote snapshot, the target implies roughly 70% upside.

The valuation screen provides another reference point, although its enterprise-value and earnings definitions need not match my model.

I would also retire the original article’s $13.50 bear case. My updated operating stress uses $75M of adjusted EBITDA, a 4x multiple, and current net cash. On a diluted share basis, that gives $22 per share. The multiple is my stress assumption.

That downside is substantial. Against the model quote, the upside-to-downside ratio is roughly 1.6 to one. It supports a position, but gives me less room for error than the original entry.

The Monte Carlo: 10,000 illustrative runs

I also tested 10,000 scenarios around the revised DCF. These are an illustrative stress analysis of the model, with explicitly chosen input distributions.

The ranges deliberately allow more deterioration than improvement. Annual growth can move six percentage points below the base path or three points above it, with the difference fading in later years. The operating margin shift ranges from four points lower to two points higher, phased in over three years. WACC ranges from 7% to 13%, with 8.6% the most likely input.

Capex, depreciation, and working capital scale with the simulated revenue. Net cash and shares remain fixed at the DCF inputs. The model uses a basic share count, so this analysis does not capture additional dilution. The unchanged-input case reconciles to the current DCF before rounding.

Most runs remain above the quote, which sits between the lower decile and lower quartile of this distribution. The median is below my target because the ranges lean toward weaker operations and a higher discount rate. The longer upper tail partly reflects how lower discount rates magnify the terminal value.

The driver analysis points to the discount rate and operating margins as the largest sources of variation within these chosen ranges. That makes the position a bet on durable cash profitability and the return the market demands for owning it.

The output tests how much room the valuation has when several assumptions move together. It cannot tell me the probability of making money: the result depends on the ranges I chose, and these scenarios do not include every possible client loss, disruption, or change in the industry’s economics. Weak growth and weaker margins could also occur together more often than the independent draws assume. The separate $22 stress case remains relevant even if it sits outside most of the simulations.

What could change my mind

The original risks remain, but their order has changed.

AI monetization comes first. The deployments are encouraging. A deterioration in existing account revenue that exceeds new AI and client revenue would undermine the argument that IBEX can grow through automation. I want clearer disclosure of that trade-off.

Margin recovery is the nearest operating test. Q1 FY2027 guidance provides an early checkpoint. If utilization improves but adjusted margins keep falling, I would question whether the problem is temporary ramp spending or weaker underlying pricing.

Cash conversion and dilution remain important. Repeatedly describing strong adjusted earnings while FCF lags would weaken the valuation. So would repurchases that largely offset stock issuance without improving per-share economics.

Client concentration and execution risks still carry weight. Healthcare growth diversifies the business, but it brings demanding data-handling and service requirements. Large client losses, operational disruptions, or a security incident could overwhelm a quarter’s new wins. A stronger balance sheet helps absorb a setback; it cannot prevent one.

Still a BUY

IBEX has delivered the growth I wanted to see. The AI case now has concrete examples, and the capital returns support continued investment. Margins are the part of the thesis that needs to catch up.

My position is unchanged. I maintain BUY and the $67 target.

The next improvement I want is more cash and profit from the clients IBEX has already won. Can management turn that larger revenue base into better per-share economics?
